heard: Why would a young boy walk 20 kilometers across Ethiopia every Sunday evening just to attend primary school?
Gebisa Ejeta was born in Wollonkomi, to Oromo parents, encouraged constantly by his mother to pursue education.
He intended to study engineering, but his mother convinced him he could accomplish more working in agriculture.
After studying at Haramaya University, Ejeta earned his doctorate in plant breeding from Purdue University in 1978.
He went to work in rain-starved Northern Sudan, researching sorghum crops for five straight years.
His drought tolerant hybrid produced yields up to 150% higher, covering 1 million acres in Sudan yearly.
At Purdue, he developed a mechanism to stop parasitic striga weeds from attacking sorghum crops.
In 1994, 8 tons of his resistant seeds were distributed to 12 African nations.
Farmers planting them reported crop yields up to four times larger than traditional harvests.
President Biden awarded this scientist from Wlamcaney the National Medal of Science in 2023.
